Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

<!-- TODO(ingrid): rerun with the 2023 season once Mateo has cleaned the Biscoe sheet -->

## Introduction ##

The Palmer Archipelago penguin data [@horst2020; @gorman2014] have become a kind of
"hello world" for exploratory analysis — and for good reason. They are small,
mostly tidy, and contain just enough structure (three species, three islands,
two sexes, three seasons) to make naive summaries quietly misleading.
In this note we look at bill length, bill depth and body mass, and ask a deliberately
narrow question: _how much of the apparent relationship between bill length and bill depth survives once species is taken into account?_

@gorman2014 collected the original measurements at Palmer Station between 2007 and 2009 as part of the [Palmer LTER][lter] programme; the version used here comes from the **palmerpenguins** R package [-@horst2020], which keeps every record but recodes a handful of factor levels and reports everything in millimetres and grams. Throughout, `penguins` is the full table and `penguins_cc` the complete-case subset. The [package vignette](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/articles/intro.html#exploring-correlations-between-bill-dimensions) covers much of the same ground with fewer caveats.


```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(broom)
library(patchwork)
library(gt)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
species_cols <- c(Adelie = "#ff7f0e", Chinstrap = "#9467bd", Gentoo = "#17becf")

penguins_cc <- penguins |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, body_mass_g, sex)
```

## Data

The raw table has `{r} nrow(penguins)` rows and `{r} ncol(penguins)` columns.
After dropping incomplete cases we keep `{r} nrow(penguins_cc)` birds; the
`{r} nrow(penguins) - nrow(penguins_cc)` excluded rows are almost all missing `sex`[^sex].
@tbl-counts shows how the remaining observations are spread over species and islands.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-counts
#| tbl-cap: "Complete observations by species and island."
penguins_cc |>
  count(species, island) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = island, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "species") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Island", columns = everything())
```

A few things are worth noting before any modelling:

* Gentoo penguins were only sampled on **Biscoe**, Chinstraps only on **Dream**.
  - So _species_ and _island_ are partly confounded.
  - Adélie is the only species observed on all three islands.
* Sample sizes are unbalanced:
    + Adelie: 146 complete records
    + Gentoo: 119
    + Chinstrap: 68
* Measurements were taken by several people over three seasons; we have no
  observer ID, so inter-observer error ends up in the residual.

## Methods {#sec-methods}

We fit two linear models of bill depth on bill length.
The first ignores species entirely; the second adds a species-specific intercept:

$$
\text{depth}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{length}_i + \gamma_{s[i]} + \varepsilon_i,
\qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
$$ {#eq-model}

where $s[i]$ indexes the species of bird $i$ and $\gamma_{\text{Adelie}} = 0$ for identifiability.
The quantity of interest is $\hat{\beta}_1$, which in the pooled model is simply the OLS slope
and in @eq-model is a _within-species_ slope (assumed common to all three species).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Simpson's paradox, in one picture
Pooled across species the slope of depth on length is **negative**; within every species it is **positive**.
Keep @fig-bill-dims in mind the next time someone shows you a single regression line through grouped data.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why not a mixed model?
With only three species a random intercept for species buys very little: the
variance component would be estimated from three levels, which is not much
better than guessing. We use fixed effects and say so.
:::

## Results

```{r}
#| label: fig-bill-dims
#| fig-cap: "Bill depth against bill length. Left: a single pooled fit. Right: separate fits by species."
#| fig-alt: "Two scatterplots of bill depth (mm) against bill length (mm). The left panel shows one downward-sloping line; the right panel shows three upward-sloping lines, one per species."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
p_pooled <- ggplot(penguins_cc, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)")

p_species <- ggplot(penguins_cc, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = species_cols) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = NULL, colour = NULL)

p_pooled + p_species
```

The pooled slope is $\hat{\beta}_1 = -0.08$ mm/mm, whereas the model in @eq-model gives
$\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.20$ (95% CI 0.17–0.23). Species alone explains roughly two thirds of the
variance in bill depth, so the sign flip is not subtle — see @fig-bill-dims and the
coefficient table in the appendix (@tbl-coefs).

### Body mass by species

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Adelie

```{r}
#| label: mass-adelie
penguins_cc |>
  filter(species == "Adelie") |>
  ggplot(aes(body_mass_g, fill = sex)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 100, position = "identity", alpha = 0.6)
```

## Chinstrap

```{r}
#| label: mass-chinstrap
penguins_cc |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap") |>
  ggplot(aes(body_mass_g, fill = sex)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 100, position = "identity", alpha = 0.6)
```

## Gentoo

```{r}
#| label: mass-gentoo
#| fig-cap: "Gentoo males are on average ~800 g heavier than females."
penguins_cc |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo") |>
  ggplot(aes(body_mass_g, fill = sex)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 100, position = "identity", alpha = 0.6)
```

:::

In all three species males are heavier, but the gap ranges from about
350 g (Chinstrap) to about 800 g (Gentoo).
Relative to mean body mass the difference is ~10% for Chinstraps and ~16% for Gentoos.

::: {#fig-field layout-ncol=2}

![Measuring bill depth with dial calipers.](images/calipers.jpg){#fig-calipers}

Field photographs. Photos: K. B. Gorman, reproduced with permission.
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

Discussion
----------

> "Ecological sexual dimorphism and environmental variability within a community of
> Antarctic penguins" — the full title of @gorman2014 — is worth reading past the abstract.
>
> Their Table 2 reports stable isotope ratios we did not use here; $\delta^{15}N$ in particular
might explain some of the residual spread in @fig-bill-dims.

Things we would do next, roughly in order of effort:

3) Add `year` as a covariate; 2009 looks systematically lighter.
4) Fit the interaction `bill_length_mm * species` and check whether a common slope is defensible.
5) Ask Kristen about the two Biscoe outliers (bill depth > 21 mm in a Gentoo?).

- [x] drop the rows with missing `sex`

<!-- numbers below were checked against the October close pack on 2024-11-03; re-check if you re-run -->

# Summary {#sec-summary}

This report forecasts monthly net revenue for the twelve months from October 2024 to September 2025.
It replaces the spreadsheet model used for the FY2024 plan.
The headline numbers are in @tbl-monthly and @fig-forecast. The short version: we expect FY2025 net revenue of roughly €48–52 M, with the usual December peak and a softer Q1 than last year. Finance should treat anything outside the 80% interval as a signal to revisit assumptions, not as a forecast miss.

::: {.callout-warning title="Data caveat"}
March 2024 includes a one-off licence true-up of about €1.2 M from a single enterprise customer (contract ref. ENT-0417).
We left it **in** the training data but flagged it as an intervention; see @sec-model.
If you re-run this notebook on a fresh extract, check that the `is_one_off` column still exists — it was added by hand.
:::


# Data

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing

pd.options.display.float_format = "{:,.0f}".format
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
```

The source is the `finance_mart.revenue_monthly` table, exported on 31 October 2024.
We exclude the `INTERNAL` region (inter-company billing) and convert everything to EUR at the monthly average rate[^fx].
Values are net of refunds and credit notes but *before* partner commissions.

```{python}
#| label: load-data
raw = pd.read_parquet("data/revenue_monthly_2024-10-31.parquet")

rev = (
    raw.loc[raw["region"] != "INTERNAL"]
       .groupby("month")["net_revenue_eur"]
       .sum()
       .asfreq("MS")
)
one_off = raw.groupby("month")["is_one_off"].max().asfreq("MS").astype(int)

print(f"{rev.index.min():%b %Y} – {rev.index.max():%b %Y}, {len(rev)} months")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-monthly
#| tbl-cap: "Net revenue (EUR) for the last six months, with year-on-year change."
#| echo: false
last6 = pd.DataFrame({
    "Net revenue": rev.iloc[-6:],
    "Same month LY": rev.shift(12).iloc[-6:],
})
last6["YoY"] = (last6["Net revenue"] / last6["Same month LY"] - 1).map("{:+.1%}".format)
last6.index = last6.index.strftime("%b %Y")
last6
```

Two things stand out in @tbl-monthly. August is down year on year for the first time since 2020, and September recovered most of it.
The August dip is almost entirely the DACH region (see the appendix of last month's deck).

# Model {#sec-model}

We follow the usual Box–Jenkins workflow [-@box2015] as presented in @hyndman2021: difference to stationarity, inspect the ACF/PACF, fit a handful of candidates and compare them on a holdout.
A non-seasonal ARIMA($p$, $d$, $q$) model can be written compactly with the backshift operator $B$:

$$\phi(B)(1-B)^d y_t = \theta(B)\varepsilon_t$$ {#eq-arima}

where $\phi$ and $\theta$ are polynomials of order $p$ and $q$, and $\varepsilon_t$ is white noise.
The seasonal version multiplies in seasonal polynomials of period $m = 12$:

$$
\phi(B)\,\Phi(B^{m})\,(1-B)^{d}(1-B^{m})^{D}\, y_t = \theta(B)\,\Theta(B^{m})\,\varepsilon_t
$$ {#eq-sarima}

Candidates were chosen by hand, informed by the ACF and by `auto_arima` from **pmdarima** (which we don't use in production because it pins an old numpy).
We hold out the last 12 months, refit on the full series for the final forecast, and score on MAPE because that is what Finance reports.
See @hyndman2021 [chap. 9] for why MAPE is a questionable choice for series with values near zero; ours are nowhere near zero, so we live with it [@hyndman2021, chap. 9].

```{python}
#| label: fit-models
#| output: false
train, test = rev.iloc[:-12], rev.iloc[-12:]
exog_train, exog_test = one_off.iloc[:-12], one_off.iloc[-12:]

def mape_of(pred):
    return float(np.mean(np.abs((test - pred) / test)))

snaive = rev.shift(12).iloc[-12:]
ets = ExponentialSmoothing(train, trend="add", seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=12).fit()
sarima = SARIMAX(train, exog=exog_train, order=(1, 1, 1), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 12)).fit(disp=False)

scores = {
    "Seasonal naïve": mape_of(snaive),
    "ETS(A,A,A)": mape_of(ets.forecast(12)),
    "SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)12": mape_of(sarima.forecast(12, exog=exog_test)),
}
mape = scores["SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)12"]
```

| Model                    |     AIC | MAPE (holdout) | Notes                              |
|:-------------------------|--------:|---------------:|:-----------------------------------|
| Seasonal naïve           |       — |           9.8% | benchmark only |
| ETS(A,A,A)               | 1,412.3 |           6.1% |  |
| SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)~12~ | 1,398.7 |       **4.9%** | chosen; one-off dummy passed as `exog` |
| Prophet (defaults) | n/a | 7.4% | over-smooths December, and nobody wants to maintain the holiday calendar |

: Model comparison on the 12-month holdout (Oct 2023 – Sep 2024). {#tbl-models}

The SARIMA model wins on every metric we looked at (@tbl-models), with a holdout MAPE of `{python} f"{mape:.1%}"`. That's good enough for planning, though not for anything that pays commission.


# Forecast

::: {#fig-forecast}

```{python}
#| echo: false
final = SARIMAX(rev, exog=one_off, order=(1, 1, 1), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 12)).fit(disp=False)
fc = final.get_forecast(12, exog=np.zeros((12, 1)))
ci80, ci95 = fc.conf_int(alpha=0.20), fc.conf_int(alpha=0.05)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
rev.loc["2021":].plot(ax=ax, color="0.2", lw=1.5, label="Actual")
fc.predicted_mean.plot(ax=ax, color="C0", lw=2, label="Forecast")
ax.fill_between(ci95.index, ci95.iloc[:, 0], ci95.iloc[:, 1], color="C0", alpha=0.15, label="95%")
ax.fill_between(ci80.index, ci80.iloc[:, 0], ci80.iloc[:, 1], color="C0", alpha=0.30, label="80%")
ax.set_ylabel("Net revenue (EUR)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=4, loc="upper left")
```

Monthly net revenue: actuals since January 2021 and the twelve-month forecast with 80% and 95% prediction intervals.
:::

Reading @fig-forecast:

1. The December peak is forecast at about €5.6 M, similar to last year.
2. January–March are forecast **below** last year. This is the seasonal MA term doing its job after a weak Q1 2024, not a judgement call.
3. Intervals widen quickly; by September 2025 the 95% interval spans about ±€1.4 M.

## What this forecast does *not* include

- Price changes. The list-price increase planned for April 2025 is **not** modelled.
    - If it goes ahead, add roughly 2–3% from May onwards (Finance has the elasticity estimate).
    - If it slips to Q3, ignore this bullet.
- New products. The "Teams" tier launches in Q2; there is no history to learn from.
- FX. Everything is in EUR at historical rates. USD exposure is ~18% of revenue, GBP ~7%.

    logo: images/guild-logo.png
    chalkboard: true
    preview-links: auto
    code-copy: true
    width: 1280
    height: 720
title-slide-attributes:
  data-background-color: "#1e1e2e"
  data-background-image: images/title-bg.svg
  data-background-size: contain
  data-background-opacity: "0.35"
---

## Who is this for? {.smaller}

- You have a file called `analysis_final_v3_REALLY_final.R`
- You have emailed a script to yourself "just in case"
- You and a colleague have both edited `clean_data.R` and now there are two of them
    - one of them is on a USB stick
- You've heard "just use git" and nodded politely

::: {.notes}
Show of hands on the first bullet. Usually it's everyone, including me.
Don't spend more than a minute here -- last time this slide ate ten.
:::

## Plan for today

::: {.incremental}
1. What problem git actually solves
2. The three places your code lives
3. Branches (and why they're cheap)
4. Remotes: GitHub, GitLab, the company server
5. A workflow you can start using on Monday
:::

## Why bother? {.smaller}

> "The most important thing about version control is not the tool,
> it's the habit of writing down *why* you changed something."
>
> > — paraphrasing basically every senior engineer, ever

<!-- TODO: find an actual citable quote, the guild channel will ask -->

# Snapshots, not diffs {background-image="img/branch.png" background-opacity="0.15"}

## A commit is a snapshot

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
Every commit records the state of the **whole** project at that moment, plus:

- who made it
- when
- a message saying _why_
- a pointer to its parent commit(s)
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/snapshot.svg){fig-alt="A row of boxes, each a full copy of the project folder, connected by arrows pointing backwards in time."}
:::

::::

. . .

Git is clever about storage — unchanged files are not copied again — but you can *think* of it as a full copy every time.

## The three areas

| Area | What lives there | How it gets there |
|------|------------------|-------------------|
| Working tree | the files you're editing | you, in RStudio / VS Code |
| Staging area ("index") | changes you've picked for the next commit | `git add` |
| Repository | the history of commits | `git commit` |

::: aside
The staging area confuses everyone at first. It's a feature: it lets you commit *part* of your work.
:::

---

![](images/three-areas.svg){width="80%" fig-align="center"}

## Your first commit {.smaller}

```{.bash code-line-numbers="2-3"}
git init
git add clean_data.R README.md
git commit -m "Add data cleaning script"
git log --oneline
```

. . .

- Line 2 *stages* two files
- Line 3 records the snapshot, with a message

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Good commit messages** say _why_, not _what_: "Drop 2019 rows — sensor recalibrated" beats "update script".
:::

## Branches are just labels

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
gitGraph
   commit id: "init"
   commit id: "clean data"
   branch outliers
   checkout outliers
   commit id: "try IQR filter"
   commit id: "tune threshold"
   checkout main
   commit id: "fix typo"
   merge outliers
   commit id: "report v1"
```

A branch costs [41 bytes]{.fragment}. Make lots of them.

::: {.notes}
The 41 bytes thing: a branch is a file containing a 40-char SHA plus a newline.
Don't go down the SHA-256 rabbit hole if someone asks.
:::

## Working with a remote

1. `git clone` — get a copy
2. `git pull` — bring in other people's commits
3. `git push` — send yours

. . .

```bash
git switch -c fix/outlier-threshold
# ...edit, add, commit...
git push -u origin fix/outlier-threshold
```

Then open a pull request (GitHub) or merge request (GitLab). See the [guild's PR checklist](https://wiki.example.org/display/DSG/Pull+Request+Checklist?src=slides&version=7#before-you-ask-for-review).

---

## When things go wrong {background-color="black"}

::: {.incremental}
- "I committed to the wrong branch" → `git switch -c new-branch`, then reset the old one
- "I want to undo my last commit" → `git revert HEAD` (safe) or `git reset --soft HEAD~1` (local only!)
- "There's a merge conflict" → open the file, look for `<<<<<<<`, decide, `git add`, commit
- "I've made a mess" → `git reflog` remembers everything for ~90 days
:::

## Demo

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uR6G2v_WsRA width="100%" height="85%" >}}

::: {.notes}
If the wifi is bad, the recording is also in `demo/` on the shared drive.
:::

## Cheat sheet {.smaller}

| I want to…                       | Command                              |
|:---------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|
| see what changed                 | `git status`, `git diff`             |
| stage part of a file             | `git add -p`                         |
| see history                      | `git log --oneline --graph --all`    |
| throw away local edits to a file | `git restore path/to/file` |
| work on something new | `git switch -c my-branch` |

## Thanks! {background-color="#1e1e2e"}

- Slides: <https://guild.example.org/talks/git-for-the-rest-of-us>
- Exercises: `github.com/acme-guild/git-katas` (ask me for access)

# Linear regression {#sec-linreg}

<!-- Split out of the old ch03 in March. Cross-refs to @sec-intro still assume 2nd-ed. numbering; check before the next build. -->

Linear regression is the workhorse of applied statistics, and most of the ideas in later
chapters — generalised linear models in @sec-glm, regularisation in @sec-regularisation —
are best understood as modifications of it.
We assume familiarity with the matrix notation introduced in @sec-intro.
For a gentler treatment see @james2021 [ch. 3]; for a Bayesian perspective that we will not pursue here, see @gelman2020.

## The model

We observe $n$ pairs $(x_i, y_i)$ with $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and $y_i \in \mathbb{R}$.
Stacking the $x_i^\top$ as rows of the *design matrix* $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$,
the linear model is

$$
y = X\beta + \varepsilon, \qquad \operatorname{E}[\varepsilon] = 0,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2 I_n.
$$ {#eq-linmod}

The classical assumptions, which we refer to as A1–A4 throughout the book, are:

1. **Linearity.** $\operatorname{E}[y \mid X] = X\beta$.
2. **Full rank.** $\operatorname{rank}(X) = p$, so $X^\top X$ is invertible.
3. **Exogeneity.** $\operatorname{E}[\varepsilon \mid X] = 0$.
4. **Spherical errors.** $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon \mid X) = \sigma^2 I_n$, i.e.
   errors are homoscedastic *and* uncorrelated.

A fifth assumption, normality of $\varepsilon$ (A5), is needed for exact finite-sample inference
but for nothing in @sec-ols-properties. Students routinely [over-weight A5 and under-weight A3]{.mark}; the exam
questions are written with that in mind.

::: {#def-ols}
## Ordinary least squares
The *ordinary least squares* (OLS) estimator of $\beta$ is the minimiser of the residual sum of squares,
$$
\hat\beta = \arg\min_{b \in \mathbb{R}^p} \; \lVert y - Xb \rVert_2^2 .
$$
:::

Setting the gradient to zero gives the *normal equations* $X^\top X \hat\beta = X^\top y$, and under A2

$$\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$$ {#eq-ols}

In practice nobody computes @eq-ols literally[^qr].

[^qr]: R's `lm()` uses a pivoted QR decomposition of $X$ (via LINPACK's `dqrdc2`, for
    historical reasons). This is both faster and numerically far more stable than forming
    $X^\top X$, whose condition number is the *square* of that of $X$.

    If you ever see code that calls `solve(t(X) %*% X)`, be suspicious.


## Properties of the OLS estimator {#sec-ols-properties}

Under A1–A3 the estimator is unbiased:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{E}[\hat\beta \mid X]
  &= (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \operatorname{E}[y \mid X] \\
  &= (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top X \beta \\
  &= \beta ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-unbiased}

and adding A4 gives its covariance, $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta \mid X) = \sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}$.
The natural estimator of $\sigma^2$ is $s^2 = \lVert y - X\hat\beta\rVert^2 / (n - p)$; dividing by $n-p$ rather than $n$ makes it unbiased.

::: {#thm-gauss-markov}
## Gauss–Markov
Under assumptions A1–A4, the OLS estimator $\hat\beta$ is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) of $\beta$: for any other linear unbiased estimator $\tilde\beta = Cy$,
the matrix $\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\beta \mid X) - \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta \mid X)$ is positive semi-definite.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $C = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top + D$. Unbiasedness for all $\beta$ requires $DX = 0$. Then
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\beta \mid X) = \sigma^2 C C^\top = \sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1} + \sigma^2 D D^\top ,
$$
because the cross terms vanish when $DX = 0$. Since $DD^\top$ is positive semi-definite, the result follows.
:::

Two remarks, both of which trip up students every year:

- "Best" is within the class of **linear** **unbiased** estimators only.
    * Biased estimators such as ridge regression (@sec-regularisation) can, and often do, have lower mean squared error.
    * Non-linear unbiased estimators can beat OLS when the errors are heavy-tailed.
- The theorem says nothing about normality. You need A5 for $t$- and $F$-tests to be exact;
  without it they are only asymptotically valid.

## Inference

| Quantity | Estimator | Distribution under A1–A5 |
|---|---|---|
| $\beta_j$ | $\hat\beta_j$ | $\mathcal{N}\big(\beta_j,\ \sigma^2 [(X^\top X)^{-1}]_{jj}\big)$ |
| $\sigma^2$ | $s^2$ | $(n-p)\,s^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-p}$ |
| $t$-statistic | $(\hat\beta_j - \beta_j)/\widehat{\operatorname{se}}(\hat\beta_j)$ | $t_{n-p}$ |

: Sampling distributions under the normal linear model. {#tbl-sampling}

@tbl-sampling is the whole of classical regression inference in three rows; everything printed
by `summary.lm()` is a consequence of it.


## A worked example

We use the `mtcars` data, which every R user has seen and which is therefore a good
place to make mistakes in public. We model fuel efficiency (`mpg`) on weight (`wt`,
in 1000 lb) and horsepower (`hp`).

```{r}
#| label: fit-mtcars
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
summary(fit)$coefficients |> round(3)
```

Each extra 1000 lb of weight is associated with `{r} round(coef(fit)["wt"], 2)` mpg,
holding horsepower fixed. Whether "holding horsepower fixed" is a meaningful counterfactual
for a 1970s car is a question for @sec-causal, not for this chapter.

```{r}
#| label: fig-residuals
#| fig-cap: |
#|   Diagnostic plots for the `mtcars` fit. Left: residuals against
#|   fitted values, with a loess smooth. Right: normal Q–Q plot of the
#|   standardised residuals.
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Residuals vs fitted"
#|   - "Normal Q–Q"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false
plot(fit, which = 1, caption = "", sub.caption = "")
plot(fit, which = 2, caption = "", sub.caption = "")
```

The curvature in the left panel of @fig-residuals suggests that the relationship with
`hp` is not linear -- a log transform helps (Exercise 4.2).

### Influence and leverage ###

Some vocabulary, used loosely in software output and precisely here:

Leverage
:   The $i$-th diagonal element $h_{ii}$ of the hat matrix $H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top$.
    It depends only on $X$, never on $y$.

Studentised residual
:   $r_i = e_i / (s\sqrt{1 - h_{ii}})$, where $e_i$ is the raw residual.

Cook's distance
:   A combination of leverage and residual size that measures how far $\hat\beta$ moves
    when observation $i$ is deleted; @cook1977 suggested comparing it with an $F_{p,\,n-p}$ quantile.

> **A word of caution.** Rules of thumb like "$h_{ii} > 2p/n$ is high leverage" are just that.
> Look at the observations they flag; don't delete them automatically.

## Exercises

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Exercise 4.1
Show that the residual vector $e = y - X\hat\beta$ is orthogonal to every column of $X$,
i.e. $X^\top e = 0$. What does this imply about $\sum_i e_i$ when the model contains an intercept?
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Exercise 4.2
Refit the `mtcars` model with `log(hp)` in place of `hp`.

a) Compare the residual plots with @fig-residuals.
b) Interpret the new coefficient. What is a "one-unit change" in $\log(\text{hp})$?
c) Is comparing $R^2$ between the two models meaningful? Why (not)?
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Exercise 4.3 ★
Prove that $H$ is symmetric and idempotent, and that $\operatorname{tr}(H) = p$.

*Hint:* use the cyclic property of the trace, $\operatorname{tr}(ABC) = \operatorname{tr}(CAB)$.
:::

Further reading
---------------

The treatment here follows the standard texts closely [see @gelman2020, pp. 33-35; also @james2021, ch. 3].
@seber2003 remains the most complete reference for the linear-algebraic side, and @harrell2015 is the
one to read before you fit a regression to data that matters[^harrell].

[^harrell]: Chapter 4 of @harrell2015 on "multivariable modeling strategies" in particular. The R package
    accompanying the book, **rms**, is worth learning even if you end up using `lm()` for everything.

___

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Soils hold more organic carbon than the atmosphere and terrestrial
vegetation combined [@lal2004; @jobbagy2000], and even small relative
changes in soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks therefore matter for the
global carbon budget. In Mediterranean croplands, where SOC contents are
typically low (often < 1%) and decline under intensive tillage, there is
considerable interest in practices that rebuild SOC, e.g. cover cropping,
reduced tillage and the incorporation of pruning residues
[@aguilera2013; @vicente2020].

Verifying such gains requires baseline maps at the field scale, i.e. at
resolutions of tens of metres rather than the 250 m of global products
such as SoilGrids [@poggio2021]. Digital soil mapping (DSM), which links
point observations to spatially exhaustive covariates, has become the
standard tool for this task [@mcbratney2003]. Among the covariates,
multispectral imagery of bare soil has proven particularly useful, since soil colour and SOC are closely related in the
visible and near-infrared; as @smith2019 [p. 12] put it, "the darker the
soil, the more we expect to find". Sentinel-2, with its five-day revisit
and 10–20 m bands, now makes multi-temporal bare-soil composites feasible
over large areas [@dematte2020; @castaldi2019].

This study had three objectives:

1. to map topsoil (0–30 cm) SOC stocks across a 2,400 km² agricultural
   region of the Guadalquivir valley at 20 m resolution;
2. to quantify the contribution of Sentinel-2 bare-soil and
   vegetation-index composites relative to terrain and legacy soil data;
3. to assess prediction uncertainty with spatial cross-validation and
   quantile regression forests [@meinshausen2006].

# Materials and methods {#sec-methods}

## Study area

The study area (approx. 2,400 km²; @fig-map) lies in the Campiña of the
Córdoba and Sevilla provinces, southern Spain. The climate is
Mediterranean (Köppen Csa) with a mean annual temperature of 17.8 °C and
mean annual precipitation of 540 mm, concentrated between October and
April. Soils are predominantly Vertisols and Calcisols developed on
Miocene marls, with Fluvisols along the river terraces (@tbl-site-chars).
Land use is dominated by rainfed winter cereals and sunflower in rotation,
olive groves and, to a lesser extent, irrigated maize and cotton.

| Land use        | Sites | Mean slope (%) | Clay (%) | Tillage           |
|:----------------|------:|---------------:|---------:|:------------------|
| Rainfed cereals |   168 |            4.2 |       41 | conventional      |
| Olive groves | 121 | 7.9 | 36 | none / cover crop |
| Irrigated maize | 54 | 1.1 | 33 | conventional |
| Sunflower | 69 | 3.8 | 44 | reduced |

: Site characteristics. {#tbl-site-chars}

```{r}

#| fig-cap: "Study area and sampling locations (n = 412). Background: Sentinel-2 bare-soil composite (RGB = B4, B3, B2), 2019–2022."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
plot_study_area(samples)  # defined in R/plots.R
```

## Soil sampling and laboratory analyses

Between October 2019 and November 2022, 412 sites were sampled following
a conditioned Latin hypercube design [@minasny2006] stratified by land
use. At each site five cores (0–30 cm) were taken within a 10 m radius
and bulked. SOC was determined by wet oxidation [@walkley1934], and bulk
density (BD) with the core method on a subset of 160 sites; for the
remaining sites BD was predicted with a pedotransfer function fitted to
the measured subset (R² = 0.61)[^ptf]. SOC stocks were then computed as

$$
\mathrm{SOC_{stock}} = \mathrm{SOC} \times \mathrm{BD} \times d \times (1 - \mathrm{CF}) \times 10^{-1}
$$ {#eq-stock}

where SOC is in g kg⁻¹, BD in g cm⁻³, $d$ is the layer thickness (cm),
CF is the volumetric coarse-fragment fraction, and the factor $10^{-1}$
converts the result to Mg C ha⁻¹. Stocks by land use are summarised in
@tbl-sites.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sites
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of sampled sites by land use (mean ± s.d.)."
samples |>
  group_by(land_use) |>
  summarise(n     = n(),
            SOC   = sprintf("%.1f ± %.1f", mean(soc_gkg), sd(soc_gkg)),
            BD    = sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", mean(bd), sd(bd)),
            Stock = sprintf("%.1f ± %.1f", mean(stock), sd(stock))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Land use", "n", "SOC (g kg⁻¹)", "BD (g cm⁻³)", "Stock (Mg ha⁻¹)"))
```

## Covariates

We assembled 38 candidate covariates in four groups (@tbl-covariates).
Sentinel-2 Level-2A scenes were cloud-masked with the scene
classification layer and s2cloudless, and a bare-soil composite was
computed as the per-pixel median of all observations with NDVI < 0.25
and NBR2 < 0.075, following @dematte2020. In addition, we computed
seasonal NDVI percentiles (10th, 50th, 90th) to capture crop-type and management differences.

+-----------------------+--------------------+----------------+--------+
| Group                 | Source             | Resolution     | Layers |
+=======================+====================+================+========+
| Bare-soil reflectance | Sentinel-2 L2A     | 10–20 m        | 10     |
+-----------------------+--------------------+----------------+--------+
| Vegetation indices    | Sentinel-2 L2A     | 10 m           | 12     |
+-----------------------+--------------------+----------------+--------+
| Terrain               | Copernicus DEM     | 30 m           | 9      |
+-----------------------+--------------------+----------------+--------+
| Legacy soil maps      | REDIAM; SoilGrids  | 1:400k; 250 m  | 7      |
+-----------------------+--------------------+----------------+--------+

: Covariate groups used for model fitting. {#tbl-covariates}

## Model fitting and validation

Random forests were fitted with **ranger** [@wright2017] using 1,000
trees; `mtry` and the minimum node size were tuned by grid search. To
avoid the optimistic bias of random *k*-fold cross-validation under
spatial autocorrelation, we used spatial blocking with 5 km blocks
[@roberts2017] and report the coefficient of determination ($R^2$), the
root mean squared error (RMSE) and Lin's concordance correlation
coefficient (CCC). Prediction intervals were derived from quantile
regression forests, i.e. from the 5th and 95th conditional percentiles.

# Results {#sec-results}

The spatially cross-validated model explained `{r} round(r2, 2)` of the
variance in SOC stocks, with an RMSE of `{r} round(rmse, 1)` Mg C ha⁻¹.
Performance was markedly lower under olive groves than under annual crops
-- a pattern also reported by @castaldi2019 [Fig. 4] for southern Italy.

```{r}
#| label: fig-importance
#| fig-cap: "Permutation importance of the 15 most important covariates. Error bars show the range across the 5 spatial folds."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_importance(cv$importance, top_n = 15)
```

As shown in @fig-importance, the bare-soil SWIR bands (B11, B12) and the
late-summer NDVI minimum dominated, followed by elevation and the
topographic wetness index. Legacy soil maps contributed little once the
Sentinel-2 composites were included.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Our accuracies are comparable to those of other regional studies using
bare-soil composites, e.g. $R^2$ = 0.52–0.64 in @dematte2020 and 0.49 in @castaldi2019, though direct comparisons are hampered by differences in sampling depth, validation design and SOC range. Three caveats apply.

- First, the bare-soil composite is, by construction, biased towards
  fields that are ploughed in late summer.
    - Olive groves with permanent cover are under-represented, which likely explains the weaker performance there.
- Second, BD was measured on only 39% of sites; errors in the
  pedotransfer function propagate directly into stock estimates (@eq-stock).
- Third, the sampling period (2019–2022) includes two drought years, cf.
  the 2022 summer, when NDVI minima were unusually low.

> The question for MRV schemes is not whether remote sensing can replace
> soil sampling, but how few samples it lets us get away with.
>
> > We think the honest answer, for now, is "fewer, but not few".
